name: Masonjoany face paste

image.caption: Malagasy girl in Nosy Be wearing masonjoany 2011

lead: Masonjoany is a traditional cosmetic paste made from grated aromatic wood mixed with water. Women in Madagascar, the Comoros and Mayotte apply it to the face for sun and insect protection, to soften and clear skin, and as decoration with painted patterns.
The paste is a long-standing cultural beauty practice. Claims of anti-aging and skin-clearing benefits are traditional, and no published study of its UV protection is cited.

paras: The wood is ground against a stone, ceramic or coral surface and mixed with water, sometimes oil, into a yellow or white paste that is applied to the face, often in patterns of dots, swirls, flowers or leaves.
No safety data were found. The main source tree is reported by Grokipedia as vulnerable due to overharvesting and bushfires.

angle.text: Wearers apply the paste for sun protection, a softer complexion and decorative patterns. The skin benefits are traditional claims rather than tested results.

lead: Masonjoany is a cosmetic paste and sunscreen made of ground wood, worn in Madagascar, the Comoros and Mayotte, where it is known as msindanu or msindzano. [1] Women use it to protect the face from sun and insects and as decoration, painting natural and abstract designs with contrasting white and yellow pastes. [1]

The yellow paste comes from the tabaky tree (Madagascar sandalwood, Coptosperma madagascariense), while white paste comes from Ficus grevei; in the Comoros Indian sandalwood is the common source. [1] Wikipedia describes the practice as stemming from exchange between Malagasy people and Indian merchants on Nosy Be from the 11th century CE, typical of the Sakalava and Vezo of the northwest coast. [1] Grokipedia (AI-generated) states that sesquiterpenoid compounds in the wood may contribute to skin effects. [2]

In Madagascar it is associated with anti-aging and cleansing, and in the Comoros with skin lightening and treating eczema, acne and allergies. These are presented as traditional beliefs, and no study of its UV protection is cited. [1]

Wood ground on stone, mixed with water

paras: The wood is ground against ceramic, stone or coral and mixed with water and oil. [1] It is worn daily for protection and for ceremonies, weddings, dances and beauty pageants. [1][2]

It is typical of the northwest coast but has spread across Madagascar, and is ubiquitous in Mayotte while declining in the Comoros. [1] Grokipedia also notes commercial lotions and creams for urban consumers. [2]
Grokipedia states that the source tree is vulnerable owing to overexploitation and bushfires. [2]
No studies found. Wikipedia notes its main scientific reference is a 2021 review of Madagascar natural products and cites no UV-protection test. [1]

timeline.event: Cultural exchange with Indian merchants at Nosy Be, to which the practice is attributed. [1]
